::: {.part}
Part one · what breathing is doing
:::

## What an ordinary rate looks like {#rates .stop data-stop="rates"}

::: {.year}
2017
:::

::: {.lead}
"Slow breathing" sounds like it must begin somewhere unusual. It begins one breath below
where most people already are.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Russo, Santarelli & O'Rourke, 2017 [@russo17] — a review of the physiology of slow
breathing in healthy people, written for a respiratory audience and free to read.

A review rather than an experiment, and the best single overview of this material. Its
authors end by saying there is "a dire need for further research into the area", which is
worth carrying through everything below.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="rates"}
Drag the rate. The same number is shown as a breath length underneath, because seconds per
breath is what anyone actually counts.
:::

The review puts an ordinary resting rate at **10 to 20 breaths a minute**, and defines slow
breathing as **4 to 10**. The two meet exactly at ten, which is the useful thing to notice:
there is no gap between normal and slow, and nothing exotic is being asked for.

At six breaths a minute — the rate the rest of this page is about — a breath takes ten
seconds. That is long enough to feel deliberate and short enough that most people can hold
it without strain. Below about four a minute the research thins out, which is why the
figure stops naming the bands there.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
"Breathe slowly" is not a useful instruction, because it has no number in it. "About ten
seconds a breath" is one, and someone can check themselves against it.
:::

## The lungs are not where the interesting part is {#oxygen .stop data-stop="oxygen"}

::: {.year}
Standard physiology
:::

::: {.lead}
Breathing harder cannot load much more oxygen onto the blood, because the blood is very
nearly full already. What changes with your breathing is how readily the oxygen comes
**off** again at the far end.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve [@dissociation] — textbook respiratory
physiology, with no single modern source to point at, so the reference is a pointer to a
standard description rather than to a study. Nothing here is contested.

The figure draws the curve from the standard equation. It is a **shape**, not measured
data, and it is a good shape: it has been the accepted description for over a century.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="oxygen"}
Move the carbon dioxide. Watch the gap between the two dots — that gap is what actually
gets handed over to the tissue, and the low end of the curve is the end that moves.
:::

Two things are worth separating here, and almost every workshop account runs them together.

**Loading.** Blood leaving healthy lungs is already carrying oxygen at something like 97 or
98% of what it can hold. The top of that curve is nearly flat, so breathing harder pushes
you along the flat part. There is very little headroom, which is why *getting more oxygen
in* is not the mechanism for anything you are about to feel.

**Unloading.** The bottom of the curve is steep, and that is the end that responds to
carbon dioxide. More carbon dioxide, and a slightly more acid blood, makes haemoglobin
loosen its grip and hand oxygen over more readily. This is the
**[Bohr effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr_effect){.wiki}**, and it points the
opposite way to most people's intuition: carbon dioxide is not simply waste to be got rid
of. It is part of how the delivery works.

So blowing off a lot of carbon dioxide shifts the whole curve leftward, and the blood holds
on tighter. Oxygen-rich blood arrives at the tissue and hands over **less** of its load.
More breathing, less delivered.

There is a real benefit at the other end of this, and the review reports it: breathing
slowly at around six a minute produced a small **rise** in blood oxygen saturation, by using
the lungs more efficiently rather than by moving more air. Slow and efficient, not fast and
hard.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
If someone on your table starts breathing big and fast because they were told deep breathing
is good, that is not a mild version of the right thing. Slower is the ingredient. Bigger,
on its own, is the next stop.
:::

## When more breathing is less {#over .stop data-stop="over"}

::: {.year}
2005
:::

::: {.lead}
The light-headed, tingling, faintly unreal feeling that comes with over-breathing is not
anxiety about the exercise. It is a measurable drop in blood flow to the brain.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Stocchetti and colleagues, 2005 [@stocchetti05], a review of deliberately induced
hyperventilation in head injury.

An odd-looking source for a page like this, and the honest one. In intensive care,
hyperventilation is used **on purpose** to narrow blood vessels in the brain and lower the
pressure inside the skull — and its known danger is cutting blood flow too far. That
establishes the direction, and that the lever is large. It says nothing about the dose
anyone gets on a mat, and the figure carries no dose for that reason.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="over"}
Directions only, no numbers. The chain is well established; how far along it any particular
person travels is not something anyone can currently put a figure on.
:::

The chain runs: breathe more than the body is asking for → carbon dioxide in the blood falls
→ blood vessels in the brain narrow → less blood reaches the brain → light-headed, tingling
hands and lips, a sense of unreality. Add the Bohr effect from the last stop and the blood
that does arrive gives up less of its oxygen.

None of that is dangerous in a healthy person doing it briefly, and it stops when the
breathing stops. It is worth knowing anyway, for two reasons. It explains a thing you will
see. And it is the clearest case on this page where *more of the good thing* is simply a
different thing.

Note what the honest version cannot say. It cannot tell you how fast is too fast, because
the evidence comes from a setting where the amount is controlled by machine and measured
directly. Anyone offering a threshold is going past their evidence.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
Tingling hands and light-headedness in a breathing exercise are a signal to slow the rate,
not to push through. The nearest thing to an antidote is an unhurried, ordinary breath — and
the person needs to be told it is a normal response to over-breathing, or they will read it
as something being wrong with them.
:::
